msContents.summary: This manuscript was brought together and partly written by one of England’s greatest historians, William of Malmesbury (c. 1090–c. 1142). He was a monk of the Benedictine abbey of Malmesbury in Wiltshire, where he acted as librarian and did more, by his own estimation, to build the collection than had ever been done before. A committed searcher of other libraries for research material, his deep interest in the Latin literature of the silver and golden ages, and his energy in identifying witnesses to different textual branches, award him a place in the history of classical transmission. This manuscript speaks to his activities as classicist and is a good specimen of his practice of setting related works together, in this case works on the art of war. It is the earliest known copy to pair Frontinus with Vegetius, a pairing which would become common from the thirteenth century. The volume has the homely appearance of other manuscripts put together by William.

msItem.note: An erased inscription in which the first word ‘Liber’ is recoverable. Written after the erasure, because it slightly impinges on it, is the titulus ‘Vegetii’ in twelfth-century majuscules; this was co-opted into the first line of a table of contents, s. xiiimed: ‘Quatuor libri Flauii Vegetii de re militari. / Quatuor libri Iulii Fronteni de exemplis rei militaris. / Decem libri breuiarium eutropii de rebus romanis. / Nomina Imperatorum.’

On an orignally blank page, a scribe using a stylish Anglicana of the mid-fifteenth century wrote a carol praising his lady’s beauty (NIMEV 2232; DIMEV 2235). It is set out as prose but is a carol of burden and three verses, as the final repetition of the first line makes plain. The dialect is assigned to Lincolnshire (LALME 1. 153). (Printed by R. H. Robbins, Secular Lyrics of the XIVth and XVth Centuries, 2nd edn (Oxford 1955), 145, no. 144 (treating it incorrectly as a song of four stanzas); and R. L. Greene, The Early English Carols, 2nd edn (Oxford 1977), 321, no. 441.1.) The same hand wrote the line on the back leaf.

p.l: My dere an dese þat so fayr ys
I kan not ly withowtyn lese
my lady lele best lyks me.
I saw neuer joy lyk to þat sight
her brows þay er both brant and bright,
Here syds er lang chapyn of ryght
be Crist & yt wer in my myght
Scho suld be my hertes sqwen
alas, sche dos me tray & teen
I may noght with her met.

msItem.note: The early-modern shelf-mark is posted at the top corner and the medieval title-piece is affixed further down (see Labels and marks). At the head of the page are two self-reflexive elegiac couplets by William of Malmesbury: ‘His sua Willelmus detriuit tempora libris, / Coniungens studiis hęc quoque parua suis. / Quos animi causa poteris percurrere lector, / Nam cum summa grauant . inferiora uiuant.’ (‘On these books William wore away his days, adding these little pieces to his studies. Peruse them, reader, to delight the mind; for when lofty works grow weighty, lesser ones stay lively.’) This is William’s own hand: Neil Ker felt that the handwriting was ‘sufficiently like his undoubted writing as to confirm rather than weaken other evidence’ (‘William of Malmesbury’s handwriting’, 66); still greater confidence is possible.

msItem.note: In William of Malmesbury’s hand, a list of emperors of the eastern and western empires, going down to John II Komnenos (1118–43) and Henry IV (1111–25). Followed by a list of the old and new names for dignities in Constantinople.

supportDesc.support: Parchment. Parchment is scrappy and poorly made, of variable thickness but with a smooth nap throughout; shiny on the hair-side, discoloured with follicles showing; whiter on the flesh. Arranged like to like, hair-side outermost. There are a number of production flaws: holes in the margin at 10, 53; holes have been written around on 6 (a slit), 18, 40 (with a long slit), 41, 90; natural edges at 6, 7, 11, 12, 16, 18, 21, 26–9, 33–4, 36–7, 39–40, 43, 47, 53, 55–6, 60–61, 65, 67, 69, 71, 76–7, 79–81, 87–92; there is neat repair stitching using different coloured thread at 14 (black), 32 (white); the stitching of 32 is exceptionally tidy, running down the length of the leaf at the outer edge as reinforcement rather than repair where the support had been weakened by scoring.

extent.measure: iii + 89 + iii folios (flyleaves are medieval parchment)

supportDesc.foliation: Foliated continuously 1–95 in early twentieth-century Bodleian pencil (as usual absorbing Coxe’s occasional numeral)
supportDesc.collation: a4 (fols. 1–3, first is pastedown) 1–610 (fols. 4–63) 710 (fols. 64–72, seventh canc., new scribe, no loss of text) 8–910 (fols. 73–92) 104 (93–95, fourth the scrappy remnant of a torn leaf). Quire signatures are found centred at the foot of the first recto, an alphabetical sequence of square capitals, A–I, K; these are in an ink blacker than the text but not looking much later.

layoutDesc.layout: Ruled in hard point for two columns of 44 lines, with an intercolumnar space of 10 mm. Outer bounding vertical rules are doubled; two single rules for the inner columns; all go the edges. Horizontal rules are doubled for first and second line at the head and antepunultimate and ultimate at the foot: these go to the edges and are ruled across the intercolumnar space; line ruling otherwise stays within the column frame. Prickings are occasionally visible at the outer fore-edge, to show they were made by awl and separately per sheet, not pricked through. Guide prickings for the vertical rules are visible in Q5. Written above top-line.

handDesc.handNote: A collaboration between six scribes, of whom one was the director of the work, William of Malmesbury, and the others, his brother monks. All write workmanlike English romanesque hands of small size, with none of the contemporary prickliness of the Canterbury/Bec styling. William wrote from 91rb line 7 to the end on 93r, and also the verses on the flyleaf (see above). He also corrected throughout. He used here his less formal register, seen also for his own Gesta regum in Magdalen 172, as established by Rodney Thomson (‘William’s “scriptorium”’, 86). The Gesta regum dates from roughly the same time in William’s career as our manuscript. Thomson’s analysis of the script recognizes three principal hands in addition to William’s, with two subsidiary efforts. The following adjusts Thomson’s account. Hand II goes from 4ra line 1 to 9vb line 16, 10ra l. 1–10rb l. 18, 10va l. 1–24rb l. 20, 24rb l. 37–25ra l. 12 (‘quadringentas’), 25va l. 1–25va l. 32, 26ra l. 26–26va l. 26, 27ra l. 1–27vb l. 34, 28ra l. 1–32rb l. 15, 32va l. 1–64rb l. 3; Hand III at 9vb ll. 17–44, 10rb ll. 19–44, 24rb ll. 20 (‘quod’)–37 (‘ordines’), 25ra l. 12–25rb l. 44, 25va l. 33–26ra l. 26 (‘pene’); Hand IV at 26va l. 26–26vb l. 44, 27vb ll. 35–44, 32rb ll. 15–44; Hand V from 64va l. 4 (first verso of quire) to 72vb; the sixth hand belongs to a man whom Thomson has dubbed Scribe A, here from 73ra (new quire) to 91rb l. 6. He is found in three other Malmesbury books, Bodl. MSS Auct. F. 3. 14 (a looser performance), Rawlinson G. 139, and Lambeth Palace, MS 224. Punctuation and abbreviation throughout is of the common sort. Ink varies between dark brown and black. Scribes were responsible for their own rubrication.

decoDesc.decoNote: Rubricated initials and headings throughout. The first initial is a plain P whose shaft descends down the margin, a total size of nine lines. Subsidiary initials for the start of chapters are a mixture of square capitals and lombards of two or three lines, variable depending on the choice of the separate scribe. Hand V produced some of his initials in black ink.

additions.p: The most frequently encountered notating hand belongs to William of Malmesbury. Some of his interventions are lexical, to show that he had access to a copy from a different textual tradition; others are corrections from knowledge, such as his interlineated note above Eutropius’s comment that Domitian died aged 35: ‘Dicit Suetonius .xlv.’ (85v). Otherwise there are nota marks throughout, apparently of twelfth- or thirteenth-century vintage. Vegetius received the most attention, Eutropius the least. A small monogram of ‘nota’ is found sporadically. At 15r in the epitome for Bk III, a coeval hand expanded the entry for c. 22 with reference to ambushes, which is what the chapter goes on to discuss: ‘superuencibus uicandis . et hostibus inferendis’. Manicules were left by different readers: on 10v, a bunched fist with horizontal index finger signals an interest sparked by the word ‘sacrament’, albeit sacraments of the military (2.5) (‘et ideo militiae sacramenta dicuntur’); a more sketchy form of pointing hand is found on 16v, 17v, 18v, 20v, 24r, taking note of utterances with a gnomic quality, e.g. ‘Saepius enim penuria quam pugna consumit exercitum, et ferro saeuior fames est’ and ‘Neque enim diuitiarum secura possessio est, nisi armorum defensione seruetur’ (both 3.3). The same emphasis applies to the interest of a different reader’s manicule on 27r, that we should only do what we judge to be useful to us (3.26). A firmly made manicule with a sleeve (36r) was drawn by the twelfth-century reader to signal the start of a new chapter. He went through and squeezed chapter numbers on to the text line or added them in the margins where the rubrication had been missed. The latest annotation by date is a partly cropped note by Robert Flemming on 85v, next to Eutropius 7.23 on the ignoble funeral of the emperor Domitian, which refers to ossuaries and the ‘strippers of corpses’ (nudatores cadauerum).

binding.p: By Roger Barnes of Oxford (d. 1631), a binding of the 1620s of reverse calf over pulpboard. Decoration on both boards is restricted to a rectilinear pattern of intersecting lines. Three-line blind fillets to the edges crossing unmitred at the corners, repeated inset at 33 mm to produce a pattern of panels, a rough square at each corner and a central panel, unembellished. Sewn on four double thongs of tanned leather, raised at the spine. Endbands of undyed thread are non-structural. Paired fore-edge ties of undyed cord are cut away flush to the boards. Fore-edges are sprinkled red. Marks of the early-modern chain-clip towards the head of the fore-edge on the lower board, with substantial verdigris on the final verso. There is the verdigris mark of an earlier chain-staple on the front pastedown, near the foot on the fore-edge. The pastedown is contiguous so has always been with the manuscript: the chaining position does not correspond to the medieval chaining at Lincoln, which seems to have been from the centre of the lower board. Twentieth-century repairs to reback the spine and make good a lost headcap; linen braids over the supports, visibly laced into the boards. Pastedown to upper board is contiguous to the text-block; so too the rear pastedown, now lifted and torn away nearly entirely.

history.provenance: The manuscript was part written, put together, and curated by the historian William of Malmesbury (c. 1090–c. 1142) monk and librarian of the Benedictine monastery at Malmesbury in Wiltshire. The dating bounds are established by the regnal lists at the back of the manuscript, copied without break from the preceding item by William himself: the last emperors in the lists are John II Komnenos (1118–43) and Henry IV (1111–25), so a date of writing between 1118 and 1125 is suggested; that accords with the date adduced from William’s citing of Frontinus and Vegetius in his Gesta regum, a work substantially complete by 1125; it need not follow that he knew them from this copy, but it would be likely. Similarities in his scribal performance between this manuscript and the autograph Gesta regum in Oxford, Magdalen College, MS 172, would bring the date of writing closer to 1125 than 1118.

Our manuscript is one of a dozen surviving autographs and represents one part of William’s activities as house librarian, a role in which he greatly augmented the monastery’s collection of books. The volume has the workmanlike appearance of other manuscripts put together under his direction; its small, bi-columnar format is very unusual for the first half of the twelfth century, but is found in other books associated with him, as Bodl. MS Auct. F. 3. 14 and Oxford, Oriel College, MS 42. Our volume represents a ‘collected edition’ of ancient texts on the art of war and bears comparison with similar collections put together by William, of Cicero’s works (CUL MS Dd. 13. 2) and computistical writings (Auct. F. 3. 14), and of texts or extracts on Roman history and law (Bodl. MS Arch. Selden. B. 16), and grammar and philosophy (BL MS Harley 3969). (See S. Niskanen, ‘William of Malmesbury as librarian: the evidence of his autographs’, in Discovering William of Malmesbury, ed. R. M. Thomson, E. Dolmans & E. A. Winkler (Woodbridge 2017), 117–27.)

The manuscript was in the hands of Robert Flemming (1416–1483), dean of Lincoln, who gave it to the College as part of his first donation in 1465, which was made up of works of classical interest. His source is not known, but the usual way a book might come free from a monastic house was into the university trade, pawned by a monk-scholar, a fifteenth-century phenomenon in particular. Flemming may not have been the first subsequent owner: the carol written on 2v has been dialectically situated in Lincolnshire, which would put it in Flemming’s diocese around the mid-century. The natural interest in this book for Flemming the humanist was that it contained old copies of Frontinus and Vegetius, not the fact that it was partly in the hand of William of Malmesbury, something he could not have known. It was in the College library in 1474 when it was reported for the third desk on the south side of the room, chained among other works of ancient history: ‘Item Vegetius de re militari et aliis ex dono eiusdem, 2o fo. sub papilionibus’ (A1. 43).

Labels and Marks. The medieval title-piece from the lower board of the medieval binding has been pasted in on fol. 3r. In the primary Textura it reads, ‘Vegetius de re militari cum Iulio Frontino ex dono Magistri Roberti Flemmyng Decani Lincoln’’. The James number ‘89’ is inked over the start of the text. Also in black ink on the fore-edge is the numeral ‘9’. The early-modern press-mark ‘E. 45. 9’ is in the top corner of 1r, repeated by a different hand on 3r. The College bookplate of 1703 is pasted at the centre of the inside front board. Beneath it is pencilled the modern Bodleian shelf-mark, ‘MS. Linc. Coll. (d) Lat. 100’. Vestiges of the paper label around the fore-edge near the head of the upper board. The Victorian pencil marks ‘Linc 100’ and ‘C 33’ (1r). On the spine, the usual square paper labels: lost at the headcap; at the foot, the blue-bordered Victorian label with ‘100’ inked on; and below that, the pale blue Bodleian printed label, mostly rubbed away.
